meta.file_purpose: Educational content for each structure drawn in the 3D prototype (src/main.cpp). Shown in the info panel when a user selects a structure.
meta.units: Metric first; imperial in brackets where the source used imperial
meta.disclaimer: Simplified educational content for a graphics prototype. Not medical advice and not for clinical use.

field_guide.summary: 2-3 short sentences. Always shown in the info panel.
field_guide.location: Where the structure sits in the body.
field_guide.functions: What it does. One short point each.
field_guide.parts: Main sub-parts a learner should know.
field_guide.numbers: Key figures, each tied to the source it came from.
field_guide.model_note: How the 3D model simplifies the real structure.

status_values.draft: Written, not yet reviewed by a teammate
status_values.reviewed: Checked by a teammate for clarity and accuracy
status_values.confirm_mapping: Team must confirm which shape in the code this entry belongs to

structures.name: Skull
structures.code_reference: drawSkeleton(): sphere at the top of the model
structures.summary: The skull is the bony case of the head. It protects the brain and gives the face its shape. Its bones are locked together by seams called sutures.
structures.location: Top of the body, resting on the first neck vertebra.
functions: Protects the brain
Protects sense organs such as the eyes and ears
Gives the head and face their shape
Provides attachment points for head and face muscles
parts: Cranium (braincase): frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid bones
Facial bones: including the nasal bones, cheekbones (zygomatic), upper jaw (maxilla) and lower jaw (mandible)
Sutures: fibrous joints between skull bones

numbers.fact: About 22 bones: 8 cranial and 14 facial
Some sutures close in infancy; others stay unfused until a person's 60s

structures.did_you_know: The lower jaw (mandible) is the only skull bone that moves.
structures.model_note: Drawn as a single smooth sphere. A real skull is made of many separate bones.

structures.name: Vertebral column (spine)
structures.code_reference: drawSkeleton(): 9 stacked spheres below the skull
structures.summary: The spine is a stack of bones called vertebrae. It holds the body upright and protects the spinal cord. Soft discs between the bones absorb shock.
structures.location: Runs down the back of the body, from the base of the skull to the pelvis.
functions: Protects the spinal cord and spinal nerves
Acts as the main weight-bearing axis, passing the trunk's weight to the legs
Allows bending and twisting
Anchors the ribs and many muscles
parts: Cervical region (neck)
Thoracic region (upper and middle back; attaches to the ribs)
Lumbar region (lower back)
Sacrum and coccyx (tailbone), made of fused vertebrae
Intervertebral discs: a gel-like centre inside a tough outer ring

numbers.fact: 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, 4 fused coccygeal
Discs make up about 25% of the spine's length
31 pairs of spinal nerves branch out between the vertebrae

structures.did_you_know: Babies are born with only some of the spine's curves. The neck curve forms when they hold up their heads, and the lower-back curve forms when they start to stand.
structures.model_note: Shows 9 rounded segments in a straight line. A real spine has 33 vertebrae and an S-shaped curve.

structures.name: Ribs
structures.code_reference: drawSkeleton(): 5 pairs of curved bones from the spine
structures.summary: The ribs are curved bones that form a cage around the chest. They protect the heart and lungs. They also move to help you breathe.
structures.location: Chest. Each rib joins the thoracic spine at the back. Most curve round to the breastbone (sternum) at the front.
functions: Protect the heart, lungs and other chest organs
Move during breathing to change the size of the chest
Anchor breathing and trunk muscles
parts: True ribs (1-7): attach directly to the breastbone by their own cartilage
False ribs (8-10): attach indirectly, through the cartilage of rib 7
Floating ribs (11-12): no front attachment

numbers.fact: Usually 12 pairs
Adults have 206 to 213 bones in total, partly because some people have extra ribs or vertebrae

structures.did_you_know: The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under the ribs, does most of the work of breathing in.
structures.model_note: Shows 5 pairs that stop short at the front. Real ribs are 12 pairs and most connect to the breastbone.

structures.name: Pelvis
structures.code_reference: drawSkeleton(): two thick bones meeting at the centre, below the spine
structures.summary: The pelvis is a ring of bones at the base of the spine. It carries the weight of the upper body to the legs. It also forms a basin that holds the bladder and reproductive organs.
structures.location: Lower trunk, between the spine and the thigh bones.
functions: Supports the weight of the upper body
Forms the pelvic cavity, which holds urinary and reproductive organs
Provides the hip sockets for the thigh bones
Forms the birth canal in females
parts: Ilium: the largest part, forming the upper wings
Ischium: the 'sit bones'
Pubis: the smallest part, at the front
Sacrum and coccyx at the back

numbers.fact: Made of five named bony parts: ilium, ischium, pubis, sacrum and coccyx

structures.did_you_know: Female pelvises are usually broader and shallower than male ones, which helps with childbirth.
structures.model_note: Drawn as two straight bars. A real pelvis is a wide, bowl-shaped ring.

structures.name: Humerus (upper arm bone)
structures.code_reference: drawSkeleton(): shoulder-to-elbow bone, left and right
structures.summary: The humerus is the only bone in the upper arm. It runs from the shoulder to the elbow. Many arm and shoulder muscles attach to it.
structures.location: Upper arm, from the shoulder to the elbow.
functions: Lets the arm move, bend and rotate
Anchors 13 muscles
Helps keep the elbow and hand stable
parts: Head: the rounded top that fits into the shoulder socket
Shaft: the long middle section
Lower end: forms the top of the elbow joint with the radius and ulna

numbers.fact: About 30 cm (1 foot) long in most adults
Longest bone in the body after the leg bones

structures.did_you_know: Hitting your 'funny bone' actually bumps the ulnar nerve, which runs just under the skin at the inner elbow.
structures.model_note: Drawn as a straight tube. The real bone has a rounded head and a wider lower end.

structures.name: Radius and ulna (forearm bones)
structures.code_reference: drawSkeleton(): elbow-to-wrist bone, left and right (drawn as one tube)
structures.summary: The forearm has two bones, the radius and the ulna. They run side by side from the elbow to the wrist. The radius rolls over the ulna so you can turn your palm up and down.
structures.location: Forearm. The radius is on the thumb side; the ulna is on the little-finger side.
functions: Let the forearm rotate (palm up, palm down)
Form part of the elbow joint
Join the wrist bones so the wrist can bend and turn
parts: Radius: thicker and slightly shorter, on the thumb side
Ulna: slightly longer, on the little-finger side; forms the bony point of the elbow

numbers.fact: Two bones in each forearm

structures.did_you_know: The bony point you lean on at the elbow is the top end of the ulna.
structures.model_note: Drawn as one tube to keep the model simple. In the body there are two separate bones.

structures.name: Hand and wrist bones
structures.code_reference: drawSkeleton(): short bone below the wrist plus 4 thin finger bones, left and right
structures.summary: The hand is built from wrist bones, palm bones and finger bones. Together they allow strong gripping and very fine movement.
structures.location: End of each arm, below the forearm.
functions: Give the hand and wrist their shape and support
Allow gripping, pinching and precise movement
Let the wrist bend and rotate
parts: Carpals: 8 wrist bones in two rows of four
Metacarpals: the palm bones
Phalanges: the finger and thumb bones
Carpal tunnel: a passage through the wrist bones for tendons and a nerve

numbers.fact: 27 bones per hand and wrist: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges
8 carpal bones, arranged in two rows of four

structures.did_you_know: Each finger has three bones, but the thumb has only two.
structures.model_note: Shows a simple palm and four fingers. There is no separate thumb or wrist bones.

structures.name: Femur (thigh bone)
structures.code_reference: drawSkeleton(): hip-to-knee bone, left and right
structures.summary: The femur is the thigh bone. It runs from the hip to the knee. It carries your body weight when you stand, walk and run.
structures.location: Thigh, from the hip joint to the knee joint.
functions: Bears body weight
Keeps the body stable when standing and moving
Anchors muscles, tendons and ligaments at the hip and knee
parts: Head: the ball that fits into the hip socket
Shaft: the long middle section
Lower end: forms the top of the knee joint

numbers.fact: About 46 cm (18 inches) long in most adults
Can support up to 30 times body weight

structures.did_you_know: The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body.
structures.model_note: Drawn as a straight tube. The real femur angles inward from hip to knee.

structures.name: Tibia and fibula (lower leg bones)
structures.code_reference: drawSkeleton(): knee-to-ankle bone, left and right (drawn as one tube)
structures.summary: The lower leg has two bones. The tibia, or shin bone, carries the body's weight. The thinner fibula sits beside it and helps steady the ankle.
structures.location: Lower leg, from just below the knee to the ankle. The tibia is on the inner side; the fibula is on the outer side.
functions: Tibia: supports body weight and links the knee to the ankle
Fibula: supports the ankle and anchors calf and leg muscles
Together: form the ankle joint with the talus bone of the foot
parts: Tibia (shin bone)
Fibula (calf bone)

numbers.fact: The tibia is the second-longest bone, about 38 cm (15 inches) in adults
The fibula does not bear body weight

structures.did_you_know: The bumps on either side of your ankle are the lower ends of the tibia (inside) and fibula (outside).
structures.model_note: Drawn as one tube. In the body there are two separate bones.

structures.name: Foot bones
structures.code_reference: drawSkeleton(): short forward-pointing bone at each ankle
structures.summary: The foot bones form arches that carry body weight. They help with balance and act like springs when you walk and run.
structures.location: Below the ankle, at the end of each leg.
functions: Support body weight when standing
Absorb shock and push the body forward when walking
Help with balance on uneven ground
parts: Tarsals: ankle and heel bones, including the talus and calcaneus (heel bone)
Metatarsals: the long bones of the middle foot
Phalanges: the toe bones
Arches: lengthwise and crosswise curves that spread weight

numbers.fact: 26 bones per foot: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges

structures.did_you_know: Together, your two feet hold about a quarter of all the bones in your body.
structures.model_note: Drawn as one short segment pointing forward. There are no separate toes or arches.

structures.name: Lungs
structures.code_reference: drawOrgans(): two tall pink-red shapes at chest height
structures.summary: The lungs are two spongy organs in the chest. They take oxygen from the air into the blood. They also remove carbon dioxide from the body.
structures.location: Chest, on either side of the heart, inside the rib cage.
functions: Bring oxygen into the blood
Remove carbon dioxide from the body
parts: Right lung: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower)
Left lung: 2 lobes (upper, lower)
Cardiac notch: a hollow in the left lung that makes room for the heart
Airways (bronchi) and tiny air sacs (alveoli)

numbers.fact: Adults breathe about 12 to 20 times per minute at rest
Right lung has 3 lobes; left lung has 2

structures.did_you_know: The right lung is shorter and wider than the left.
structures.model_note: Drawn as two smooth ovals of equal size. Real lungs differ in size and lobes.

structures.name: Heart
structures.code_reference: drawOrgans(): orange-red shape between and below the lungs
structures.summary: The heart is a muscular pump in the chest. It pushes blood through the blood vessels to every part of the body. It has four chambers and four valves.
structures.location: Front of the chest, between the lungs, slightly left of centre, behind the breastbone.
functions: Pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body
Pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs
Helps keep blood pressure steady
parts: Two upper chambers: right and left atria
Two lower chambers: right and left ventricles
Four valves: tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary and aortic
Its own electrical system that sets the heartbeat

numbers.fact: About the size of a fist
Weighs about 280 g (10 ounces) on average

structures.did_you_know: The heart's valves are one-way doors. They stop blood from flowing backwards.
structures.model_note: Drawn as a single smooth oval. The real heart has four chambers and is cone-shaped.

structures.name: Kidneys
structures.code_reference: drawOrgans(): pair of tan shapes below the heart (CONFIRM with team)
structures.summary: The kidneys are two bean-shaped organs near the back of the abdomen. They filter waste and extra water from the blood to make urine. They also help control blood pressure.
structures.location: Upper back of the abdomen, one on each side of the spine, just below the rib cage.
functions: Filter waste and extra fluid from the blood
Make urine
Help control blood pressure
Make hormones, including one that triggers red blood cell production
Help balance the blood's acidity (pH)
parts: Nephrons: tiny filtering units
Renal artery: brings blood in
Ureter: carries urine to the bladder

numbers.fact: About 10-13 cm (4-5 inches) long, roughly fist-sized
Over 1 million nephrons in each kidney
Filter about 190 litres (200 quarts) of fluid a day, but make only about 2 litres (2 quarts) of urine

structures.did_you_know: Almost all the fluid the kidneys filter is taken back into the body. Only about 1% leaves as urine.
structures.model_note: Drawn as two simple ovals in front of the spine. Real kidneys sit towards the back of the body.

structures.name: Urinary bladder
structures.code_reference: drawOrgans(): purple shape at the lowest point, inside the pelvis (CONFIRM with team)
structures.summary: The bladder is a stretchy, hollow organ in the pelvis. It stores urine from the kidneys until you go to the toilet. Its muscular wall squeezes to empty it.
structures.location: Lower abdomen, inside the pelvis, behind the pubic bone.
functions: Stores urine
Signals the brain when it is filling
Squeezes to push urine out
parts: Inner lining (urothelium): stops urine leaking into the body
Connective tissue layer with vessels and nerves
Thick muscle wall made of three layers of smooth muscle

numbers.fact: Holds about 500-700 mL (about two cups)
The urge to urinate usually starts at about 200-350 mL
About 5 cm (2 inches) across when empty; can stretch to about 15 cm (6 inches)

structures.did_you_know: You feel the need to go well before the bladder is full.
structures.model_note: Drawn as a fixed oval. A real bladder changes size as it fills and empties.

structures.name: Aorta
structures.code_reference: drawVessels(): central vertical tube running down the body
structures.summary: The aorta is the body's largest artery. It carries oxygen-rich blood away from the heart. Smaller arteries branch off it to reach every part of the body.
structures.location: Starts at the heart, arches over it, then runs down through the chest and abdomen to the pelvis.
functions: Carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the body
Feeds branches that supply the head, arms, organs and legs
parts: Ascending aorta: rises from the heart's left ventricle
Aortic arch: curves over the heart
Descending thoracic aorta: runs down the chest
Abdominal aorta: runs through the abdomen and splits into the iliac arteries

numbers.fact: About 2.5 cm (1 inch) wide at its widest point
More than 30 cm (1 foot) long

structures.did_you_know: The aorta is elastic. It stretches with each heartbeat and then springs back, helping to keep blood moving.
structures.model_note: Drawn as a straight vertical tube. The real aorta starts with an arch over the heart.

structures.name: Arteries of the arm
structures.code_reference: drawVessels(): branches from the top of the aorta to each shoulder, elbow and wrist
structures.summary: These arteries carry blood from the aorta down to the arms and hands. The main vessel changes its name as it travels. At the elbow it splits in two.
structures.location: From the top of the chest, through the armpit and upper arm, to the forearm and hand.
functions: Supply oxygen-rich blood to the shoulder, arm, forearm and hand
parts: Subclavian artery: under the collarbone
Axillary artery: in the armpit
Brachial artery: down the upper arm to the inner elbow
Radial artery: elbow to the thumb side of the wrist
Ulnar artery: elbow to the little-finger side of the wrist

numbers.fact: The brachial artery splits into two branches at the elbow crease: radial and ulnar

structures.did_you_know: A blood pressure cuff squeezes the brachial artery. You check your pulse at the wrist by pressing on the radial artery.
structures.model_note: Drawn as one tube per arm. In the body the artery splits into two at the elbow.

structures.name: Arteries of the leg
structures.code_reference: drawVessels(): branches from the bottom of the aorta down each leg
structures.summary: These arteries carry blood from the aorta down to the legs and feet. The aorta splits into the iliac arteries in the pelvis. These continue as the femoral arteries in the thighs.
structures.location: From the lower abdomen, through the pelvis and groin, down the thigh to behind the knee and into the lower leg.
functions: Supply oxygen-rich blood to the hips, thighs, legs and feet
parts: Common and external iliac arteries: in the pelvis
Femoral artery: down the thigh
Popliteal artery: behind the knee
Arteries of the lower leg and foot

numbers.fact: The femoral artery is usually 7-8 mm wide

structures.did_you_know: Doctors often thread thin tubes (catheters) through the femoral artery to reach the heart, because it is wide and easy to reach.
structures.model_note: Drawn as one tube per leg. Real leg arteries branch many times.
